title: A Rare Case of Lambert-Eaton Myasthenia Syndrome Associated with Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma: A Case Report and Review of the Literature
case_prompt:
A 57-year-old man with a 2-month history of lepromatous leprosy treated with rifampicin, clofazimine, and dapsone presented with abdominal distension, constipation, vomiting, and a 10-kg weight loss. He was vitally stable, with peripheral lymphadenopathy and a distended abdomen with shifting dullness. Abdominal CT showed terminal ileal mural thickening, enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes, mesenteric fat stranding, and free intraperitoneal fluid, suggesting either granulomatous infection or a neoplastic process. Paracentesis revealed atypical large lymphocytes; flow cytometry showed an abnormal CD4/CD8 double-negative T-cell population (38%) with multiple aberrancies. Cervical lymph node biopsy confirmed high-grade peripheral T-cell lymphoma, and bone marrow was uninvolved. He was staged as IV and started on dexamethasone. After developing severe sepsis requiring one week in the ICU, he recovered and received six cycles of dose-adjusted EPOCH chemotherapy with intrathecal methotrexate. After four cycles, PET/CT showed complete metabolic remission, but he had multiple episodes of febrile neutropenia and bacteremia.  

During this admission, he developed progressive, generalized weakness without sensory changes or clear fatigability. Neurologic examination showed symmetric proximal and distal muscle weakness (Medical Research Council grade 3/5) with preserved sensation and reflexes. Given his ICU stay, neurotoxic drug exposure, and malignancy, the differential diagnosis included critical illness myopathy–neuropathy, toxic neuropathy, and paraneoplastic syndrome.  

Nerve conduction studies showed normal distal motor latencies, normal compound muscle action potentials, normal conduction velocities, and normal F-waves in all motor nerves. Sensory nerve studies revealed normal onset latencies, normal sensory nerve action potential amplitudes, and normal conduction velocities. Needle electromyography of proximal and distal muscles in all limbs exhibited normal insertional activity, no spontaneous activity, and normal motor unit action potentials, but with poor recruitment. Finally, repetitive nerve stimulation at 30–40 Hz elicited a marked incremental response, suggesting a presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Critical illness myopathy–neuropathy was considered due to the ICU stay but excluded as EMG showed normal muscle membrane activity — “...exhibited normal insertional activity, no spontaneous activity, and normal motor unit action potential...”  
2. Toxic neuropathy was considered given neurotoxic chemotherapy but excluded because sensory studies were intact — “sensory nerve studies revealed normal onset latencies, normal sensory nerve action potential amplitude, and normal conduction velocities.”  
3. A presynaptic paraneoplastic neuromuscular junction disorder (LEMS) was supported by the characteristic high-frequency incremental response — “repetitive nerve stimulation (at 30–40 Hz) showed a significant incremental response ... suggesting a presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder (likely LEMS).”
